ak_sunny_side_the.blurb: A mellow sport wall at Worthington Glacier on Thompson Pass, tucked on the back side of a steeper neighboring cliff. The climbing is mostly long, easy to moderate bolted lines, with a scattering of trad and top-rope options, so it suits newer leaders and anyone after a relaxed day of volume. Most routes sit around 5.7 and the range runs from low 5th class to about 5.11, with stainless anchors. The wall catches afternoon sun. Expect a glacier backdrop, a stream crossing on the approach, and loose scree on the trail, so keep your feet dry and watch the footing on the walk out.
ak_sunny_side_the.parking_note: Park in the Worthington Glacier State Recreation Site lot off the Richardson Highway on Thompson Pass.
ak_sunny_side_the.approach: From the lot, follow the paved path past the viewing platform, cross the meltwater stream (a tyrolean is rigged), then walk downstream to the lake and follow a cairned trail along the toe of the buttress, over a few scree fields, to the ledge below the wall.

ak_keystone_canyon_2.blurb: A narrow, wind-scoured gorge carved by the Lowe River a short drive from Valdez, and one of the best-known waterfall ice venues in Alaska. Nearly all of the climbing is frozen waterfalls with dense blue ice, many of them multi-pitch and visible from the road, plus a mixed line or two. Grades run from easy WI2 and WI3 flows through a good handful of WI4 and WI5 classics, with a few harder test pieces. Walk-ins to the base are short, usually under ten minutes. The highway runs through the canyon and can be icy, and falling ice from above is a real concern on the bigger flows.
ak_keystone_canyon_2.approach: Most flows are a 5 to 10 minute walk from the highway pullouts; a few need a crossing of the Lowe River.

ab_wasootch_slabs.blurb: A small, low-elevation slab crag in the Kananaskis Valley, close to Calgary and long a favorite for learning. The south-facing slabs are split into lettered sections, and while the area is best known for top-roping, there are also sport leads and a few trad lines. Many routes are in the 5.4 to 5.7 range, with a solid number of 5.9 to 5.11 lines mixed in. It dries fast and gets strong sun, so it is one of the first crags usable in late winter and a warm pick in spring and fall. The lower slabs are polished in places, so friction can feel slick, and it gets busy on fine weekends.
ab_wasootch_slabs.parking_note: Heading south on Highway 40 from the Trans-Canada toward Barrier Lake, pull into the Wasootch Creek day-use lot on your left and leave the car there.
ab_wasootch_slabs.approach: A short, easy walk of roughly a kilometer or less up the creek bed on a faint trail leads to the first slabs; the others are reached along their base.

ab_upper_wall.blurb: The hardest sector at Acephale, a shaded limestone crag on the flank of Heart Mountain near Canmore. The Upper Wall is steep and overhanging, with shorter, more intense sport routes than the lower sector and a couple of big caves. Nearly everything here is 5.11 or harder, with plenty of 5.12 and 5.13, so it is a destination for strong climbers. The rock is blocky, blue-streaked and rough on the skin, and tape helps. It sits in shade all day, which makes it a good summer choice and a cold place for belaying in shoulder seasons. The approach is a steep uphill trail, with the Upper Wall about ten minutes past the lower sector.
ab_upper_wall.parking_note: From Canmore, drive toward Calgary past the Lac des Arcs exit for about 2 km and turn into the large dirt pullout near a guardrail and ponds on the right.
ab_upper_wall.approach: Follow the signed, steep uphill trail from the pullout to the lower sector, then continue up and right for about ten more minutes to the Upper Wall.

az_overlook_the.blurb: A trad crag at the top of Oak Creek Canyon on Highway 89A, a short drive south of Flagstaff, built from broken columnar basalt. It is known for a large number of moderate crack and corner lines with only a few hard test pieces, which makes it a good place to build lead experience. Most routes fall between 5.8 and 5.10, with fewer 5.7s and 5.11s. The wall faces southeast and goes into shade in the early afternoon. There are no fixed anchors on the main wall, so bring rope to rig a top-out or rappel.

az_east_side.blurb: The east side of Winslow Wall, a varnished sandstone canyon wall on East Clear Creek south of Winslow. It is overwhelmingly steep sport climbing with a few trad lines, on good rock with a hard dark patina. The grades are strong: most routes are 5.11 and 5.12, with a handful of 5.10s and almost nothing easy, and the style leans to patina crimps, stemming scoops and technical faces. It is a long drive and a committed approach that ends in a rappel on fixed lines, so it feels remote and quiet. The canyon can flash during monsoon storms, spring water is often high and late fall is cold, so late spring through mid fall is best. Watch for poison ivy.
az_east_side.parking_note: From Winslow, take Highway 99 east about 6 miles, crossing the Fort McHood bridge, then follow dirt roads beside a fence to the end of the road, roughly three quarters of a mile past a fork. Stay on the established road, which crosses private and ranch land, and close gates as you found them.
az_east_side.approach: Walk about a third of a mile along the canyon rim to a slot, scramble down, and rappel the fixed lines to the canyon floor. To leave, jug the ropes, climb the rappel gully (about 5.4), or top out from routes that reach the rim.

az_apache_leap.blurb: A huge band of volcanic cliffs forming the skyline east of Superior, in the Queen Creek area. Climbing is mostly bolted sport with a few trad lines, and the middle section holds the tallest walls in the canyon, with routes of up to six pitches. The grades are spread across 5.7 to 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. Expect exposure and a sense of adventure, and helmets are a good idea. Approaches vary by section and are long, some using rough dirt roads that need high clearance or 4WD, or a cairned hike with rappels from the top. Many sections face west and southwest, so they are sunny in the afternoon. Take care near the cliff edge.
az_apache_leap.parking_note: The north end is reached from the small lot at the end of Magma Mine Road, just before the mine entrance fence. Other sections use rougher dirt roads that may need high clearance or 4WD.
